articles.text: Mrs. J. B. Raymond, wife of Dakota's delegate to Congress, was buried Feb. 22. Mrs. Raymond has been an invalid for over six years. Many expressions of condolence were received by Mr. Raymond and the funeral was attended generally by both houses of Congress. The interment took place at Rock Creek cemetery.
articles.summary: Mrs. J. B. Raymond, wife of Dakota's delegate to Congress, was buried at Rock Creek cemetery on Feb. 22.

articles.text: In spite of severe losses, the BXB outfit on the South Moreau is not at all discouraged. They have recently bought a large outfit in Nebraska and this season will drive up 10,000 beef cattle on their Moreau range. We wish them every success.
articles.summary: The BXB outfit on the South Moreau, despite severe losses, has bought a Nebraska outfit and will drive 10,000 beef cattle to its Moreau range this season.

articles.text: The warm weather which began yesterday is hailed with joy by every one as the first harbinger of approaching spring. The cattlemen especially are rejoicing as it will put a stop to losses already larger than usual unless some entirely unexpected weather ensues. A regular chinook wind set in early this morning and two more days will completely clear the ground of snow.
articles.summary: Warm weather and a chinook wind ended the cold snap, to the relief of cattlemen whose losses were already larger than usual.

articles.text: It may be a little inappropriate at this time to "lock the stable door after the horse is stolen" by drawing a moral from the accident to Frank Walker yesterday morning, but it seems necessessary to say something. The thoughtlessness of some people in handling fire-arms is simply criminal carelessness and should be punished the same as any other crime. There is no excuse for leaving a load in the barrel of a Winchester at any time as the cartridge can be thrown into the barrel from the magazine and the gun cocked with as quick a motion as the single one of raising the hammer.
articles.summary: Editorial drawing a moral from Frank Walker's rifle accident: careless handling of fire-arms should be punished like any other crime.

articles.text: Mr. O. H. Holt of Bismarck, private secretary to Gov. Pierce, has published a pamphlet on Dakota, which is full of valuable information to any one desiring to learn our resources. One of the extracts written by the editor of the Cow Boy in his tenderfoot days contains the information that cattle paw away the snow to get at the grass in winter. A settled conviction has come over our minds that this should be taken with a grain of allowance, perhaps two grains wouldn't do any harm. In all other respects the pamphlet is a model of compact information and should be in the possession of everyone who wishes to learn or give information about Dakota.
articles.summary: Packard praises O. H. Holt's pamphlet on Dakota resources, while doubting his own tenderfoot-era claim in it that cattle paw away snow to reach grass.

articles.text: As a sort of addenda to our remarks on the river, may be mentioned the fact that last Saturday, when the weather was below zero here, word came that there was a raise of three or four feet of water coming, and at that time was about twenty-five miles up the river. The flood is travelling at the rate of four or five miles a day and will probably be here to-night or to-morrow. It may seem strange that although there is a pitch of over two thousand feet to the river, the flood does not come faster. This is accounted for by the fact that the channel is very crooked and that the ice is covered with snow which must all be melted thus reducing the water to a kind of thin slush.
articles.summary: A rise of three or four feet of water reported last Saturday 25 miles up the Little Missouri was expected at Medora that night or the next day.

articles.text: From M. S. & F. Co., October 5, one sorrel horse; four white feet, white stripe in face, branded -Y- on left shoulder and [box brand] on left thigh. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery.
articles.summary: Medora Stage & Forwarding Co. offers $25 for a sorrel horse strayed October 5.

articles.headline: Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text:
From my ranch on Little Missouri, ten miles south of Medora, the night of November 19, a dark sorrel mare, weighing about nine hundred pounds, left front knee stiff, white and red scar on left side, far back, brand M bar on left hip. Mare about nine years old. The finder will be paid for his trouble by leaving information leading to her recovery with me.

A. Young, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: A. Young advertises a dark sorrel mare strayed or stolen from his ranch ten miles south of Medora on November 19.

articles.headline: Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: $25 reward for John Pohl's bay horse strayed or stolen from Little Missouri on July 6, 1884.

articles.text: The cattle and horse business in the Bad Lands has passed the experimental stage and there is no doubt that they are unsurpassed for both purposes. As a horse country especially, it has many advantages not present in other sections. The soil is of such a nature that the quality of the hoofs constantly improves and no better quality can be found anywhere than on horses reared here. The winters are just cold enough to make the horses hardy and still not so cold as to hinder the largest growth of blooded stock. For wind, however, this climate is superior to any other. It is dry, light and considerably rarer than at the sea level. This latter fact will at some time be of great value if our horsemen raise racing stock. If in a comparatively rare atmosphere a horse's wind is good, it stands to reason that it will be better in a denser atmosphere.
articles.summary: Editorial note boosting the Bad Lands as horse country: hard hoofs, hardy winters and thin dry air good for wind.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts has already made a contract to deliver four hundred head of cattle to Glendive. The contract is made with the same firm to which he delivered cattle there last year and which was so well satisfied that they voluntarily paid yearling prices for some calves born on the road.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts has contracted to deliver 400 head of cattle to Glendive.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a letter from Dan Friedman, who is now at Cold Spring Minn. He don't enlarge much on the use of side-saddles but mentions that he is having a first-rate time. He is a partner of Lloyd Roberts in buying cattle and states that cattle there are at the lowest notch, nine to ten dollars for yearlings and fourteen to sixteen for two-year-olds.
articles.summary: Dan Friedman, Lloyd Roberts' cattle-buying partner, writes from Cold Spring, Minn., that yearlings sell there for $9-10 and two-year-olds $14-16.

articles.text: Beef is selling now from Helena to St. Paul at 10½ cents by the side and exceedingly hard to get, even at those figures. Why do not some of our enterprising stock men cut out a herd of their heavy beef cattle in the fall, and hold them for these high winter markets? Good hay can be secured during the summer and the cattle can be held on a pasture, reserved for that purpose, when the grass gives out, the cattle can be made to keep their flesh on hay, at least until the first of March. The hay of this country cut in season and properly cured is nearly as fattening as grain. Who will try the expirement next year?
articles.summary: With beef at 10½ cents from Helena to St. Paul, the paper urges stockmen to hold heavy beef cattle on hay for the winter market.

articles.text: The breeders of Aberdeen-Angus cattle in this country have so far done but little showing at our fat-stock shows, having necessarily but very few pure-bred animals to show. As it is, they point with just pride to the record they have made in proportion to their numbers. In 1883, Black Prince worthily upheld, almost unassisted, the honor of the breed. This year some younger animals came to his assistance. In spite, however, of the slimness of their exhibits, they have well sustained their reputation as prize winners, especially in the carcass classes—the block test, that feature of our fat stock shows which our English friends commend so highly. In 1883, with two of this breed slaughtered out of nineteen, Aberdeen-Angus took first prize in the two-year-old class, at Chicago. At the Chicago show of 1884, there were thirty animals slaughtered, of which four were Aberdeed-Angus grades, two of which took firsts in the two-year-old and yearling classes respectively. At Kansas City, last fall, the Angus men, as will be remembered by most of our readers, were justly jubilant over the record of Pride 3d of Blairshinnock, Burleigh's Pride and Abernethy, the latter, the same which, at Chicago, stood first in the two-year-old carcass class. In proportion then to the numbers exhibited both in live and carcass classes, but especially in the latter, the Aberdeen-Angus cattle have a record to be proud of.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprint from the National Live Stock Journal on the prize record of Aberdeen-Angus cattle at Chicago and Kansas City fat-stock shows.

articles.headline: Roller Skating.
articles.text:
This amusement has become the most popular indoor amusement of the day and doubtless many will be interested in knowing of its origin and subsequent history.

Roller skating is no new thing. Roller skates were patented and used in France in 1819. A few years later an Englishman by name of Syers invented and manufactured them in England. The Syers skate was a sandal placed on fi[ve?] wheels in a single row and arranged s[o?] that only two wheels touched the floor at one time.

The Plympton skate was the first patented in the United States, about the close of the civil war, and the first public rink was opened in Newport R. I. in 1866. It is still in existence. The "skating craze" sprung from this city rapidly all over the country. In '73-'74 it died down again in the United States but was was fully sustained in European countries, and in the East Indies and Australia raged more fiercely than in more northern countries.

In 1880 the interest in roller skating revived in the New England states and has since been rapidly spreading toward the Pacific slope, until nearly every town of eight hundred inhabitants or more in the eastern states has a roller rink and very many of the southern and western towns and cities are also supplied with this rapidly increasing popular amusement. The chief advantage of roller over ice skating is that the amusement in roller rinks may be indulged in during any season of the year, in well lighted and heated halls. In ice skating, it can only be indulged in during a very small portion of the year and at considerable risk to life and health.

There is an essential difference of motion between ice and roller skating. On ice it is a glide, and on rollers it is the motion of walking.

The first lesson on rollers, is to walk without allowing the skates to roll.

A beginner must become firmly impressed with the idea that "haste makes waste." Confidence is the first element of success and a few falls at the out-set are quite apt to make people more or less timid.

To attain grace and perfection in skating a careful study of the first movements and positions are very essential, in fact the more difficult movements cannot be gracefully performed without a thorough mastery of the rudiments. As there is soon to be a new roller rink built at Medora, we would suggest to our young people, and old ones to for that matter, that they provide themselves with "Spalding's manual" and if they will follow its instructions closely we will guarantee that they will not regret it in the future.
articles.summary: History of roller skating with advice for beginners, ending with the news that a new roller rink is soon to be built at Medora.

articles.headline: An Interesting Story.
articles.text:
The following story, coming home to all readers of the Cow Boy as concerning a well-known character formerly living here, will be found full of interest.

Seven years ago, the subject of our sketch was living in a small eastern village, supporting by his labor an invalid father and mother. In this, he was assisted by a sister and between them they barely succeeded in gaining enough to supply food for the family. The boy, then fourteen years old, was eager to learn a trade and [get?] an education, but poverty compelled him to put them off.

An old friend of the family had come out to this country and engaged extensively in cattle raising. He was very successful and going back east on a visit, called on our hero's family. Seeing their poverty stricken condition, he immediately offered the boy whose name was Stephen, a position on his ranch at a salary more than he could possibly make at home. The offer was gladly accepted and Stephen, although immediately nicknamed the "Kid" became a valuable hand, as he was quick to learn and eager to please. Round-ups followed each other in rapid succession and last year Stephen was acknowleddyed to be one of the best cow-boys that rode the range. He grew in favor with his employer and and was then appointed foreman of his outfit.

Comfort at last came to the "old folks' at home" for the "Kid" regularly sent the most of his salary to supply their wants. The future looked bright and everything went along peacefully until late last fall, when the "Kid" and a bosom friend were driving in a bunch of cow-horses from a distant round-up. They were sleeping near the bunch and were awakened in the night by a band of rustlers who had stampeded the herd except two horses which were kept hobbled near camp. The "Kid" and his pard rushed to saddle up and start in pursuit. As it happened, two of the best horses had been kept up and as dawn was just breaking it was an easy matter to follow rapidly on the trail. An hour or two's hard riding brought them in view of the band and although there were five of the horse thieves, neither of the cow-boys thought of the odds but spurred their horses harder than ever to catch up. The thieves saw the boys at almost the same time and riding around a butte, two of them cached themselves and the others drove on with the herd. Just as they rounded the butte they were saluted by a discharge from the rifles of the rustlers. One of the balls struck the Kid in the breast knocking him from his horse and the other killed his pard's horse. The robbers, thinking both men were killed rode after the herd. The Kid's partner extricated himself from under his horse and hastening to his chum's side had only time to receive his dying words: "Take large envelope from—pocket and send to father."

The chum did as requested and accompanied his friend's body to the east. It was a mournful mission, as he had to inform the grief stricken family that their only support was taken from them. The loss of their dearly beloved son, poverty without hope and the poor-house as a sole refuge was a sickening prospect. The chum could offer no consolation and forgot the envelope entirely until after the funeral. Thinking of it then, he gave it to the father and imagine the flood of joy that overcame him at the thoughtfulness of his son when he found that it contained a policy for $5,000 in the safety fund department of the Hartford Life and Annuity insurance company. Sabe?
articles.summary: A story, presented as concerning a cowboy "formerly living here," of the "Kid" Stephen, shot by horse rustlers, whose family was saved by his $5,000 Hartford Life policy; it reads as an insurance reading-notice.

articles.text: Tommy Smith accompanied Russ Wilson to the E6 ranch and will again hold down a position as cow-puncher.

articles.text: Arch. Boyd intends leaving the Pyramid Park hotel the first of March and J. B. Walker will take his place as host. Mr. Boyd has in many ways shown himself a valuable citizen and we are pleased to state, intends remaining with us.

articles.text: The Rev. Mr. Scheffner, of Dickinson, came down Sunday evening, expecting to preach. Arrangements had not been made, however, and the meeting was postponed to some future time. We hope to see more of the gentleman.
articles.summary: Rev. Mr. Scheffner of Dickinson came to preach but the meeting was postponed.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens, wife and sons came in on yesterday morning's coach from Cave Hills. The Dr. has already begun house-keeping. We are pleased to welcome this family to Medora and we know that the members will become prime favorites. The Dr. is thinking seriously of putting in a herd of cattle.
articles.summary: Dr. H. M. Jorgens and family arrived from Cave Hills and have set up housekeeping in Medora.

articles.text: Every Studebaker wagon we have sold has given the best of satisfaction and those wishing new ones would do well to give us a call. We have a number of 3-inch wagons just right for round-up use. The 3½-inch wagon will hold up as much as can be piled on and is guaranteed for 5,000 pounds. No better ironed and braced wagons are made than the Studebaker.
articles.summary: Reading notice for Studebaker wagons suited to round-up use.

articles.text: The snow is over a foot deep on the level, a heavier fall than there has been within the memory of the oldest inhabitant. All things considered, the cattle are doing well but from recent reports, the loss may be heavier than was expected. It is of course, impossible to state the loss accurately but our estimate of five per cent. as an outside loss may be realized.
articles.summary: Snow over a foot deep, the heaviest in memory; cattle loss may reach the paper's outside estimate of five per cent.

articles.text: M. M. and Mrs. Coleman celebrated their eighteenth wedding anniversary, the evening of the twenty-second. There was a large attendance of friends and many were the expressions of good will to the host and hostess. A thoroughly enjoyable time was had by all, the only disappointment being that eighteenth wedding anniversaries do not come eighteen times a year instead of once in eighteen years.
articles.summary: M. M. and Mrs. Coleman celebrated their 18th wedding anniversary on Feb. 22 with a large party.

articles.text: Geo. Wilkes returned from Chicago last Friday where he purchased all the machinery for the new slaughter house. The boilers are of the Buckeye pattern and George says the whole plant was just what he wanted. No expense was spared in getting the best, the total cost in Chicago amounting to nearly $8,000. Gorge also brought with him a superior Claybrough gun which we know by experience is a fine shooter.
articles.summary: George Wilkes returned from Chicago with nearly $8,000 of machinery for the new slaughter house.

articles.text: It will be remembered that last fall Bill Jones arrested a man near Scoria cut for setting the grass on fire. Jones took the man to Mandan, made out the complaint and left the criminal in jail. Soon afterward the report came that he had been released and was found nearly frozen to death between here and Glendive. This report is now changed, and by good authority the man is said to be still in the Mandan jail. Something should be done in this case immediately. Jones is entitled to the reward offered for the arrest of anyone setting fire to the grass, when up to the present time he has not even had his expenses paid. The board of the prisoner is a constant expense that Billings county will at some time have to pay. The total costs now amount to about $20[illegible] and it is time this useless expense was stopped.
articles.summary: The man Bill Jones arrested last fall near Scoria cut for setting a grass fire is still in the Mandan jail; Jones has not been paid the reward or expenses.

articles.text: Geo. Wilkes wants it distinctly understood that no one shall take anything from the slaughter-house without his permission. Several tools are missing that he needs badly.
articles.summary: George Wilkes warns against taking tools from the slaughter-house.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock will immediately begin the erection of a first-class livery stable, 38x50 feet. The building will have drop siding, battlement front, two-inch ground floor, matched flooring to the hay loft and will be located on third street between Third avenue and Broadway.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock will build a 38x50-foot livery stable on Third street between Third avenue and Broadway.

articles.text: Frank Walker was the victim of an extremely painful accident yesterday morning. He accidentally shoved his leg against a loaded rifle which was lying on a chair, in such a way that the hammer was pushed against a round of the chair and the rifle was discharged. The ball entered the leg just below the knee and shattered both bones. A very ugly wound was made and it is doubtful if the leg can be saved, although the attending physician, Dr. Robart will try to do so. Frank has the sympathy of the entire community and they all join in wishing him a speedy recovery.
articles.summary: Frank Walker shattered his leg below the knee when a loaded rifle on a chair discharged; Dr. Robart may not be able to save the leg.

articles.headline: Good Bye
articles.text:
By Jennie Wilkes.

Oh, how sad to see the red lips quiver,
The bright eyes filled with tears,
When two young hearts are parting
Forever or for many years.
The hands are clasped so tightly,
Tears on the white cheek lie,
When the last, last words are spoken:
Remember me—good bye.

I look in vain for the sweet blue eyes,
I breathe on the wind her name;
Oh, would that the echo might bring
That form to me again.
But the echo is all that I hear;
In vain for her I sigh;
I have watched that light form out of sight;
Oh, sad is the word, good-bye.

And memory calls forth another one
So haughty and so fair;
Her eyes like diamonds flash,
And jet black is her hair.
But I love the blue eyes better,
For gold her heart did buy;
She is linked by a golden fetter,
And we have said good-bye.

And oh! so many are gone
Where the sun shall never set;
Their eyes are closed forever
With tears to be never wet.
I have felt the clasp of many a hand,
Which cold in the grave now lie;
The lips are closed which uttered:
God bless you, Jennie, good-bye

So it is with all on earth—
We all must laugh and cry;
We never know how dear one is
Till we have said good-bye.
[illegible] as others live,
[illegible] [cal?]led to die,
[illegible] [pa?]ss to another world,
[illegible] said good-bye.

[illegible — editor's note partly covered by a dark band] ... [writt?]en by the youngest daugh[ter] [illegible] [wh?]en but thirteen years old. For one so young, it shows superior poetical ability.—Ed.]
articles.summary: Poem "Good Bye" by Jennie Wilkes, with an editor's note that it was written by a youngest daughter of about thirteen; the last stanza and part of the note are hidden by a dark band on the scan.

articles.text:
The following is the constitution of the Gun club as adopted last evening. All who wish to shoot must be on hand promptly at 1:30 Saturday afternoon as the contest will begin on time:

Constitution and By-laws of the Bad Lands Gun Club.

Sec. I. The name of this association shall be "The Bad Lands Gun Club."

Sec. II. The object of this association shall be to further the interests of rifle, shot-gun and revolver practice.

Sec. III. Membership in this association shall be obtained by receiving a majority of votes in any meeting containing a quorum of the association and by signing the constitution and paying the treasurer the sum of one dollar.

Sec. IV. Provided the weather will permit, weekly contests will be held on every Saturday afternoon, beginning at 1:30. The preliminaries and the kind of contest or contests to be decided by the executive committee.

Sec. V, Art 1. Rifle contests to be at ranges decided upon by the executive committee, provided they do not exceed one thousand yards, and to be subject to military rules. Each contestant to use the same gun at the several ranges, globe and peep sights barred except as permitted by military rules. Each contestant to have five shots at each range. Each contestant to pay the treasurer the sum of fifty cents before each contest or he is not entitled to shoot. The contestant having the highest average in any series of five contests to be awarded a new rifle not to exceed $25 in price. Each contestant when in town and able to shoot to be obliged to enter every contest in the series. Any contestant when unable to attend any contest may, at the option of the executive committee, shoot before them under the same rules as govern other contests to take place of the omitted contest.

Art. 2. Shot gun contests to be under the rules of Bogardus clubs.

Art. 3. Revolver contests to be at ranges not to exceed one hundred yards. Targets and ranges to be decided upon by the excutive committee governed by the same general rules as rifle contests, the prize to be a revolver not exceeding $15 in price.

Sec. VI. All disputes to be decided first by the executive committee and then by the next meeting of the association.

Sec. VII. This constitution to be amended by a three-quarters vote of any regular meeting having a quorum of the association, provided: the amendment is presented in writing and read at a previous meeting.

Sec. VIII. Membership fees to be used only for running expense of the club.

Executive committee:
A. T. Packard,
E. G. Paddock,
J. N. Maxwell.
articles.summary: Constitution and by-laws of the new Bad Lands Gun Club, adopted Feb. 25, with weekly Saturday contests; executive committee Packard, Paddock and Maxwell.
